title.narrative: Fostering Ownership Resources Capacities and Enablement for Refugees

description.narrative:
The FORCE4Refugees project aims to recognize the expertise, autonomy and potential of refugee organizations (Refugee Led Organizations - RLOs) and civil society (CSOs) active in the field of migration and displacement.
Equal partnership, collaboration and customization characterize the project's approach. The project aims to provide these organizations with the tools, resources and skills to address the challenges faced by refugees, migrants and host communities.
The project is based on three main intervention strategies: A component to the to strengthen capacityIn this component, RLOs and CSOs determine their own priorities. A component for direct financingThrough this component, RLOs and CSOs receive the funding to implement the plans made. A component for meaningful participationThrough this component, the project aims to amplify the voice of refugees and RLOs.

title.narrative: 1a Contribution to improvement of policy frameworks for hosting refugees aligned with international legal frameworks

comment.narrative: Refugees under Temporary protection face significant insecurity and barriers linked to registration, mobility, verification procedures, and uneven local implementation. Access to work permit is structurally limited, with refugees largely confined to informal labor markets. No clear long-term legal framework for Syrians wishing to remain.
No evidence yet as this period consisted of the inception phase of the project, implementation has not begun yet

Refugee led organisations (RLOs) such as iGAM and DOOR engaged directly with policymakers through structured consultations, parliamentary meetings, and a pioneering Memorandum of Understanding with the Gaziantep City Assembly. At national and global levels, F4R’s expanded presence in Geneva enabled RLOs to convey field-based evidence and recommendations during the Global Refugee Forum Progress Review, contributing to more informed and inclusive policy discussions. These efforts collectively supported an environment where refugee rights and legal frameworks were increasingly discussed with direct RLO input, contributing to gradual improvements in policy coherence and responsiveness.

title.narrative: 1b Contribution to better implementation of existing ILF-aligned laws and policies

comment.narrative: Refugees under Temporary protection face significant insecurity and barriers linked to registration, mobility, verification procedures, and uneven local implementation. Access to work permit is structurally limited, with refugees largely confined to informal labor markets. No clear long-term legal framework for Syrians wishing to remain.

Implementation of protection and legal frameworks improved through RLO-led service delivery, technical engagement with authorities, and strengthened coordination systems. Olive Branch’s legal aid centre ensured consistent access to legal guidance, helping refugees navigate documentation procedures and prevent loss of status. The establishment of structured communication channels between RLOs and provincial Migration Directorates enabled faster, clearer case referrals and smoother application of existing regulations. By supporting complex cases, including deportation risks, GBV, and child protection, partners helped ensure that ILF aligned laws were applied more consistently and equitably in practice.
No evidence yet as this period consisted of the inception phase of the project, implementation has not begun yet

title.narrative: RA2: Forcibly displaced people and members of their host communities have improved access to quality services.

description.narrative: RESULT AREA 2: Improved access to basic services for FDPs and host community members (HCMs)

title.narrative: 2.1 Contribution to improved access to basic services, education, social protection and critical infrastructure

comment.narrative: Qualitative baseline: access to services remains uneven, with significant barriers for those residing outside their registration provinces. Refugees faced widespread discrimination and legal uncertainty in accessing education, healthcare, and social protection.
No evidence yet as this period consisted of the inception phase of the project, implementation has not begun yet

Throughout the reporting period, partners helped expand access to essential services for both forcibly displaced people and host community members by strengthening community‑based service provision and filling gaps left by the downscaling of international actors. Olive Branch provided consistent child‑focused psychosocial support and strengthened referral pathways to MHPSS providers, ensuring continuity of care for vulnerable children. Women Now broadened access to education and social cohesion opportunities through vocational gastronomy workshops, gender‑equality panels, and art‑based psychosocial activities in public schools, reaching children from diverse backgrounds. iGAM complemented these efforts by organising community events and countering misinformation through active media outreach. Together, these interventions contributed to more accessible, community‑rooted, and inclusive service environments for refugees and host communities, improving overall well‑being and reducing barriers to essential support.

description.narrative: RESULT AREA 4: Global, institutional and national level policies and practices allow for more effective and efficient usage of development funding

title.narrative: 4 Contribution to a change in the aid ecosystem facilitating increased, more effective and efficient usage of development funding in refugee responses

comment.narrative: RLOs continued to face ill-conceived, one-size-fits-all capacity strengthening requirements, limited access to flexible funding, and tokenistic participation in policy processes at local, national and international levels. In Türkiye specifically, Syrian-led and refugee-led organisations faced structural barriers linked to legal registration, unequal positioning within the aid architecture, and direct access to funding.

A central achievement was the production of a Joint Policy Note, co authored with NEAR Network, RRLI, RPW, and PASC, which articulated a shared set of recommendations on direct and equitable funding for refugee led actors. Its recommendations were delivered to donor embassies at the high level forum of the GFRPR.

title.narrative: 4e Evidence of joint programming/policy work leading to improved refugee policy frameworks

comment.narrative: The UNlobal Compact on Refugees (GCR, 2018) had explicitly recognised that responses are most effective when they actively and meaningfully engage those they protect, and the Netherlands had signed a refugee participation pledge committing to systematically include refugees in programme design and to promote RLO resilience and agency. Despite these commitments, RLOs continued to face ill-conceived, one-size-fits-all capacity strengthening requirements, limited access to flexible funding, and tokenistic participation in policy processes at local, national and international levels. In Türkiye specifically, Syrian-led and refugee-led organisations faced structural barriers linked to legal registration, unequal positioning within the aid architecture, and direct access to funding.

Joint policy work directly contributed to improved visibility of refugee perspectives within national and global policy frameworks. The production of a widely endorsed joint policy note with NEAR Network, RRLI, RPW, and PASC presented unified recommendations on equitable funding, influencing donor conversations at the GRFPR. By securing RLO participation in high level platforms previously inaccessible to them, F4R ensured that refugee generated evidence fed directly into policy discussions. This led to increased attention to RLO leadership, localisation, and more inclusive approaches to policy design among donors and UN agencies.
No evidence yet as this period consisted of the inception phase of the project, implementation has not begun yet

title.narrative: 4c Evidence of partners increasing frequency of joined-up planning, programming and reporting

comment.narrative: the global refugee regime is under unprecedented pressure, with 108.4 million forcibly displaced people worldwide including 35.3 million refugees. The UN Global Compact on Refugees (GCR, 2018) had explicitly recognised that responses are most effective when they actively and meaningfully engage those they protect, and the Netherlands had signed a refugee participation pledge committing to systematically include refugees in programme design and to promote RLO resilience and agency. Despite these commitments, RLOs continued to face ill-conceived, one-size-fits-all capacity strengthening requirements, limited access to flexible funding, and tokenistic participation in policy processes at local, national and international levels. In Türkiye specifically, Syrian-led and refugee-led organisations faced structural barriers linked to legal registration, unequal positioning within the aid architecture, and direct access to funding.

Joint advocacy missions, shared stakeholder mapping exercises, and coordinated messaging around the GRFPR reinforced coherence across organisations. This collective approach resulted in streamlined programming, strengthened coherence in partner reporting, and greater alignment of advocacy priorities across the coalition.
No evidence yet as this period consisted of the inception phase of the project, implementation has not begun yet
